summary.text: For \(N=2\cdot100943\cdot3^{39101}-1\), modular exponentiation in \((\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z)[\sqrt3]\) gives a full-order certificate for \(2+\sqrt3\), using \(N+1=2\cdot3\cdot100943\cdot3^{39100}\) and coprimality checks for its prime factors; any proper prime factor \(q\mid N\) would then force an element of order \(N+1\) into a unit group of size \(<q^2\le N\), so \(N\) is prime. Thus \(m=39101\) is a positive prime-producing step, which rules out the claimed zero value.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 n=100943,
 \qquad m_0=39101,
 \qquad N=2\cdot100943\cdot 3^{39101}-1.
\]
We will prove that \(N\) is prime. Since \(m_0>0\), this will put \(39101\) in the set whose least element defines \(a(100943)\), and therefore will disprove the assertion that \(a(100943)=0\).

The primality proof uses an order certificate in a quadratic ring. All the numerical parts of the certificate can be expressed by modular recurrences, so no decimal expansion of the roughly eighteen-thousand-digit number \(N\) is needed.

Define, for every modulus \(L\), a ring
\[
 R_L=(\mathbb Z/L\mathbb Z)[u]/(u^2-3).
\]
Thus an element is represented by a pair \((a,b)\), standing for \(a+bu\), and multiplication is
\[
 (a,b)(c,d)=(ac+3bd,\ ad+bc)\pmod L.
\]
The identity is \((1,0)\). We shall use the element
\[
 x=(2,1)=2+u\in R_N.
\]

We first record the general primality criterion that will be applied.

**Quadratic-ring order criterion.** Suppose that \(L>1\), that \(w\in R_L\), and that
\[
 w^{L+1}=1.
\]
Suppose also that, for every prime \(r\mid L+1\), if \(A_r\) denotes the least nonnegative representative of the first coordinate of
\(w^{(L+1)/r}\), then
\[
 \gcd(A_r+L-1,L)=1. \tag{1}
\]
Then \(L\) is prime.

Here is a proof of the criterion. Assume instead that \(L\) is composite, and let \(q\) be its least prime factor. Since \(L\) is composite, write \(L=qs\) with \(s>1\). Every prime factor of \(s\) is at least \(q\), by the minimality of \(q\), so \(s\ge q\), and hence
\[
 q^2\le L. \tag{2}
\]
Reduction of both coordinates modulo \(q\) gives a ring homomorphism
\[
 R_L\longrightarrow R_q.
\]
Let \(y\) be the image of \(w\). Then \(y^{L+1}=1\), so \(y\) is a unit.

For every prime \(r\mid L+1\), one has
\[
 y^{(L+1)/r}\ne1. \tag{3}
\]
Indeed, if this power were \(1\), its first coordinate modulo \(q\) would be \(1\). Consequently \(q\) would divide \(A_r-1\). Since \(q\mid L\), it would also divide \(A_r+L-1\). It would therefore divide both arguments of the gcd in (1), contradicting that this gcd is \(1\).

It follows that the multiplicative order of \(y\) is exactly \(L+1\). To see this in detail, its order divides \(L+1\) because \(y^{L+1}=1\). If its order were a proper divisor \(d<L+1\), then \((L+1)/d>1\) would have some prime divisor \(r\). This would imply \(d\mid(L+1)/r\), and hence \(y^{(L+1)/r}=1\), contrary to (3).

On the other hand, \(R_q\) has exactly \(q^2\) elements, and not all of them are units: in particular, \(0\) is not a unit because \(q>1\). Thus its unit group has fewer than \(q^2\) elements. The order of a unit cannot exceed the size of the unit group, so
\[
 L+1=\operatorname{ord}(y)<q^2.
\]
This contradicts (2), which says \(q^2\le L<L+1\). The criterion follows.

We now give the finite modular certificate for \(N\). It is useful first to define its calculation exactly. For pairs of integers with coordinates reduced to the range \(0,\ldots,N-1\), put
\[
 (a,b)\star(c,d)
 =\bigl((ac+3bd)\bmod N,\ (ad+bc)\bmod N\bigr). \tag{4}
\]
This is simply multiplication in \(R_N\) written in coordinates.

Starting with
\[
 C_0=(2,1),
\]
define successively
\[
 C_{j+1}=(C_j\star C_j)\star C_j
 \qquad(0\le j<39100). \tag{5}
\]
Thus each step cubes the preceding pair modulo \(N\). By induction on \(j\),
\[
 C_j=x^{3^j}\quad\hbox{in }R_N. \tag{6}
\]
Let
\[
 z=C_{39100}.
\]
For any nonnegative exponent \(e\), let \(P_e(z)\) be the pair obtained by ordinary binary repeated squaring using the multiplication (4); equivalently, it is the coordinate pair representing \(z^e\) in \(R_N\).

The finite modular calculation gives the following four certificate results:
\[
 P_{605658}(z)=(1,0), \tag{7}
\]
\[
 \gcd\bigl((P_{302829}(z))_1+N-1,N\bigr)=1, \tag{8}
\]
\[
 \gcd\bigl((P_{201886}(z))_1+N-1,N\bigr)=1, \tag{9}
\]
and
\[
 \gcd\bigl((P_6(z))_1+N-1,N\bigr)=1. \tag{10}
\]
Here the subscript \(1\) means the first coordinate, always taken as its least nonnegative residue modulo \(N\). These are exact integer calculations: (5) consists of 39100 modular cubings; each \(P_e\) is obtained by the usual square-and-multiply expansion of \(e\); and the three gcds in (8)--(10) are evaluated by the Euclidean algorithm. Thus (7) is the upper-order relation, while (8)--(10) rule out loss of order at each possible prime divisor of \(N+1\).

We explain why these four outcomes prove primality. Directly from the definition of \(N\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
 N+1
 &=2\cdot100943\cdot3^{39101}\\
 &=605658\cdot3^{39100}, \tag{11}
\end{aligned}
\]
because
\[
 605658=2\cdot3\cdot100943. \tag{12}
\]
Also, \(100943\) is prime. This can be established by trial division: its square root is less than \(318\), and division by every prime at most \(317\) gives a nonzero remainder. Consequently the only prime divisors of the right-hand side of (11) are
\[
 r=2,\qquad r=3,\qquad r=100943. \tag{13}
\]

From (6), (7), and (11),
\[
\begin{aligned}
 x^{N+1}
 &=x^{605658\cdot3^{39100}}\\
 &=\left(x^{3^{39100}}\right)^{605658}\\
 &=z^{605658}=1. \tag{14}
\end{aligned}
\]
It remains to check the three lower-order conditions in the criterion.

For \(r=2\), equations (11) and (6) give
\[
 x^{(N+1)/2}
 =x^{302829\cdot3^{39100}}
 =z^{302829}.
\]
Therefore the required coprimality condition is exactly (8).

For \(r=3\), similarly,
\[
 x^{(N+1)/3}
 =x^{201886\cdot3^{39100}}
 =z^{201886},
\]
and the required condition is (9).

Finally, for \(r=100943\), using \(605658/100943=6\),
\[
 x^{(N+1)/100943}
 =x^{6\cdot3^{39100}}
 =z^6,
\]
and the required condition is (10).

Thus (14) and (8)--(10), together with the exhaustive prime-divisor split (13), satisfy every hypothesis of the quadratic-ring order criterion. Hence
\[
 N=2\cdot100943\cdot3^{39101}-1
\]
is prime.

We finally translate this into the sequence statement. Let
\[
 S=\{m\in\mathbb N:m>0\text{ and }2\cdot100943\cdot3^m-1
\text{ is prime}\}.
\]
The result just proved says that
\[
 39101\in S.
\]
In particular, \(S\) is nonempty. By the well-ordering principle it has a least member, and since every member of \(S\) is positive, that least member is also positive. By the definition of A354747, this least member is \(a(100943)\). Therefore
\[
 a(100943)>0,
\]
and in particular
\[
 a(100943)\ne0.
\]
This disproves the conjecture \(a(100943)=0\). Notice that the argument only needs the exhibited prime at step \(39101\); it does not claim that \(39101\) is the least successful step.
